summary:
FuegoClaro is a web application that helps users explore satellite thermal detections across mainland Ecuador and the Galapagos Islands. Developed by team SputinkSP, it addresses the Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots challenge by organizing NASA FIRMS records into a common structure while preserving each sensor's identity and original confidence information.

The application connects an interactive map, a monthly calendar, seasonal views, and a sensor comparison dashboard. Users can filter by location, date, sensor, and confidence, then export records to reproduce their analysis. Its documented dataset contains 116,729 detections from January 2022 to November 12, 2026.

FuegoClaro helps students, researchers, and environmental analysts identify spatial and temporal patterns without treating different sensors as equivalent. Complementary modules explore thermal event grouping and protected-area intersections. The project emphasizes responsible interpretation: thermal detections are not confirmed wildfires, detection counts do not measure burned area, and predictive outputs require independent validation.
details:
Project overview

FuegoClaro was developed by team SputinkSP for Challenge 09: Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots. It is a web application for exploring satellite thermal detections in mainland Ecuador and the Galapagos Islands through an interactive map, a hotspot calendar, statistical summaries, and sensor comparisons.

The problem

MODIS and VIIRS differ in spatial resolution, sensitivity, and confidence representation. Comparing their raw detection counts without considering these differences can lead to misleading conclusions. Combining UTC timestamps, local dates, geographic boundaries, and standard and near-real-time products also creates challenges for reproducible analysis.

Our approach

FuegoClaro organizes NASA FIRMS observations into a common data structure while preserving sensor, satellite, source product, and original confidence information. The processing pipeline validates records, removes duplicate identifiers, clips observations to Ecuadorian boundaries, and derives local dates for mainland Ecuador and the Galapagos Islands.

Confidence categories support filtering but are not presented as equivalent calibrated probabilities across sensors. The project harmonizes data structure, time, geography, and selection criteria; it does not perform radiometric calibration or turn MODIS and VIIRS into a single instrument.

Main features

Users can explore detections on an interactive map, inspect daily activity in a monthly calendar, examine seasonal patterns, and compare MODIS and VIIRS under shared geographic and temporal filters. The dashboard summarizes detection counts and distributions. Data exports, URL-based filters, and dataset metadata support reproducibility, while a methodology page explains processing decisions and limitations.

Complementary modules provide spatiotemporal grouping of thermal detections, exclusion of observations near catalogued gas flares before event grouping, protected-area intersections, and experimental susceptibility estimates. These functions depend on the geographic data and model artifacts available in the deployment. Their outputs support exploration and prioritization for further review, not confirmation of emergencies.

Data and reproducibility

The dataset documented in our technical report contains 116,729 detections: 20,382 MODIS and 96,347 VIIRS records, covering January 1, 2022, through November 12, 2026. A processing manifest records source products, transformations, exclusions, coverage, and a SHA-256 checksum. Exported records and an audit script support independent reproduction of descriptive counts.

Technology

The backend and processing pipeline use Python, FastAPI, Pandas, NumPy, and Shapely. Experimental machine-learning components use scikit-learn. The frontend uses React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Leaflet, and Recharts. Docker Compose and Nginx support containerized deployment.

Creativity and intended impact

FuegoClaro connects where detections occur, when they occur, and how sensor records differ within one traceable workflow. Its contribution is not simply displaying satellite points, but helping users interpret those points without hiding differences between sensors.

Potential users include students, researchers, environmental analysts, local governments, and emergency-management teams reviewing historical activity. The intended benefit is easier access to interpretable satellite information. Operational improvements, such as faster response or reduced losses, have not yet been measured.

Scientific limitations

A thermal detection is not a confirmed wildfire. Detection counts do not measure burned area, establish the cause of a thermal anomaly, or represent a count of unique fires. Missing detections do not prove the absence of fire. Experimental predictions estimate detection-derived activity and require independent and prospective validation. FuegoClaro does not replace field verification or official emergency services.

Future work

Planned improvements include scheduled FIRMS updates, clearer observation-availability indicators, independent validation against incident records, human feedback from field teams, and notifications through institutional communication channels. These are future developments rather than established operational capabilities.

AI assistance disclosure

The team used Codex and OpenCode for coding assistance and implementation alternatives, and Antigravity to support role planning and task distribution. AI tools also supported documentation and discussions about model selection. Team members reviewed and adapted the outputs and retained responsibility for the project concept, implementation decisions, interpretation, and final submission. NASA FIRMS observations were not generated by these assistants. The experimental predictive model is separate from the generative AI tools used during development.
